# Introduction and Overview

The primary objective of this process is to transform three independent, wide data sets into formats ready for downstream analysis. Wide data sets are retrieved as .CSV files. The three selected data sets include synthetic Business Cost and Revenue data, 2022 US Census data, and World Bank Life Expectancy data. Each data set, after import, will be tidied according to standard conventions. Certain aspects of each data set will be analyzed: from the World Bank Data, rates of life expectancy growth across regions could be compared, while the US Census data could be analyzed for population growth momentum, and cost and revenue temporal trends could be determined for the business data set.

Anticipated challenges include initial import of unwieldy .CSV files. For instance, some may have header text that must be ignored when importing. Additionally, the World Bank data is separated into three distinct .CSV files, so joining these sets together as data frames may be necessary.

# Approach

1.  Import each data set
2.  Tidy each data set
3.  Analyze each data set
4.  Visualize each data set
5.  Present findings and recommendations for each data set

# Codebase

## Data Import

### Data Sources

Data set 1 (2022 US Census data) was sourced from a discussion board post by [Anastasiia Gmyrina](https://brightspace.cuny.edu/d2l/le/1344368/discussions/threads/5805589/View). Data set 2 (Business Costs Revenue data) was sourced from a discussion board post by [Jocelyn Slater](https://brightspace.cuny.edu/d2l/le/1344368/discussions/threads/5777654/View). Data set 3 (World Bank Life Expectancy data) was sourced from a discussion board post by [Ummay Rukiya](https://brightspace.cuny.edu/d2l/le/1344368/discussions/threads/5847178/View). Data set 3 requires multiple imports for multiple .CSV files, and certain files have header information that requires skipping those rows.

```{r data-import}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

url_1 <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kailot-harris/DATA-607-Project-2/refs/heads/main/data/census_top10_states_2022_untidy.csv"

url_2 <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kailot-harris/DATA-607-Project-2/refs/heads/main/data/5A_BusinessCostsRevenue.csv"

url_3a <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kailot-harris/DATA-607-Project-2/refs/heads/main/data/API_SP.DYN.LE00.IN_DS2_en_csv_v2_460061.csv"

url_3b <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kailot-harris/DATA-607-Project-2/refs/heads/main/data/Metadata_Country_API_SP.DYN.LE00.IN_DS2_en_csv_v2_460061.csv"

url_3c <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kailot-harris/DATA-607-Project-2/refs/heads/main/data/Metadata_Indicator_API_SP.DYN.LE00.IN_DS2_en_csv_v2_460061.csv"

csv_data_1 <- readr::read_csv(file = url_1, 
                            show_col_types = FALSE,
                            progress = FALSE)

csv_data_2 <- readr::read_csv(file = url_2, 
                              show_col_types = FALSE,
                              progress = FALSE)

csv_data_3a <- readr::read_csv(file = url_3a, 
                               show_col_types = FALSE,
                               skip = 4,
                               progress = FALSE)

csv_data_3b <- readr::read_csv(file = url_3b, 
                               show_col_types = FALSE,
                               skip = 0,
                               progress = FALSE)

csv_data_3c <- readr::read_csv(file = url_3c, 
                               show_col_types = FALSE,
                               skip = 0,
                               progress = FALSE)
```

## Data Transformation

The raw .CSV data for data set 1 is transformed initially by cleaning the names, renaming a few columns, and removing the `rank` column. This column was removed because it provided a numerical rank that would be rendered meaningless during the subsequent transformation: the frame is pivoted longer and a new date column is created to capture the old variable names.

```{r transform-1}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_1 <- csv_data_1 |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>                               # clean names
  rename(area = geographic_area,                          # rename area
         april_1_2020 = april_1_2020_estimates_base) |>   # rename april_1
  select(-rank)                                           # remove rank column

df_1b <- df_1 |>
  pivot_longer(            
    cols = 2:4,                                           # columns to pivot
    names_to = "dates",                                   # names become dates
    values_to = "count"                                   # values become count
  ) |>
  mutate(dates = mdy(dates))                              # dates reformatted

df_1c <- df_1b |>
  group_by(dates) |>                                      # group by dates
  mutate (total = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),               # sum across dates
          prop = count/total,                             # calc proportion
          months = interval(ymd("2020-04-01"),dates) / months(1)  # define months since estimate base
  )

df_1d <- df_1c |>
  group_by(area) |>                                       # group by area
  arrange(dates, .by_group = TRUE) |>                     # arrange by date within group
  mutate(
    count_growth = (count-lag(count))/(months-lag(months))/1000, # Thousands of pop growth/month
    prop_growth = (prop-lag(prop))/(months-lag(months))*100      # Prop growth %age
  ) |>
  ungroup()

knitr::kable(head(df_1d))
```

The raw .CSV data for data set 2 is transformed initially by cleaning the names, renaming a few columns, and removing the `feb_cost_k` and `march_cost_k` columns after recasting them into the same units as the other columns. The frame is pivoted longer and a new date column is created.

```{r transform-2}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_2 <- csv_data_2 |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate (feb_cost = feb_cost_k *1000,      # recalc cost
          march_cost = march_cost_k *1000   # recalc cost
          ) |>
  select(-c(feb_cost_k, march_cost_k))      # remove columns
  
df_2b <- df_2 |>
  pivot_longer(
   cols = -c(location, name),               # not location nor name
   names_to = c("month", ".value"),         # make months and cost/rev columns
   names_sep = "_"                          # column name separator
  )

year <- as.integer(2026)                    # define year
day <- as.integer(1)                        # define day

df_2c <- df_2b |>
  mutate(
    month_num = match(                      # find month number
      str_sub(str_to_lower(month), 1, 3),   # use first three lower case letter
      str_to_lower(month.abb)               # compare to abbreviations for months
    ),
    date = make_date(year, month_num, day), # make date column
    profit = revenue-cost,                  # make profit column
    ppc = profit/cost                       # calc profit per cost
  ) |>
  select(date,                              # select needed columns
         name, 
         location, 
         cost, 
         revenue, 
         profit, 
         ppc)

knitr::kable(head(df_2c))
```

Upon inspection, it appears a data entry error occurred in the data for Bobby in Boston from May. The reported revenue is \$6,150,000, while the cost is only \$25,000. Before fixing this entry error, a check will be performed to see if any other values exceed reasonable limits.

```{r inspect-df_2c}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_2c <- df_2c |>
  arrange(desc(revenue))

knitr::kable(head(df_2c))
```

Only that single row contains misleading data. Next, the data error is fixed using an `if_else()` function to match the row to its descriptors.

```{r fix-df_2c}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_2c <- df_2c |>
  mutate(
    revenue = if_else(              # replace using if logic
      name == "Bobby" &             # match name
        location == "Boston" &      # match location
        month(date) == 5 &          # match month
        revenue == 6150000,         # match revenue
      61500,                        # replace revenue
      revenue),                     # else:: keep same revenue 
    profit = revenue - cost,        # redefine profit
    ppc = profit / cost             # redefine ppc
  )

knitr::kable(head(df_2c))
```

The raw .CSV data for data set 3 is transformed initially by removing unnecessary columns: an extra, empty column with a header containing the string "...", and indicator code and name columns. These columns were removed because they contained redundant information. Next, the frame is pivoted longer and the names are cleaned. A new date column is created to using January 1st for each year.

```{r transform-3}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_3 <- csv_data_3a |>
  select(-starts_with("...")) |>    # Remove extraneous column
  select(-c("Indicator Code",       # Remove indicator code column
            "Indicator Name"))      # Remove indicator name column

df_3b <- df_3 |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c("Country Name",       # pivot the country name
              "Country Code"),      # pivot the country code
    names_to = "Year",              # make new column year
    values_to = "Life Expectancy"   # make new LE column
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()            # clean names

month_num <- as.integer(1)          # set january

df_3c <- df_3b |>
  mutate(
    date = make_date(year,          # create date 
                     month_num, 
                     day),
  )

knitr::kable(head(df_3c))
```

Before joining data from the second .CSV file in data set 3, a data frame is formed by selecting only the necessary columns and cleaning their column names. Then, the two data frames from each of the first two .CSV files of data set 3 are joined by the country code.

```{r transform-3b}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_4 <- csv_data_3b |>
  select(c("Country Code",       # keep columns
           "Region", 
           "IncomeGroup")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()         # clean names

df_3d <- df_3c |>
  left_join(                    # join dfs
    df_4, by = "country_code"   # by country code
  ) |>
  arrange(date)                 # sort by date

knitr::kable(head(df_3d))
```

## Analysis

### Data set 1: US Census Data 2022

First, the data set is summarized by determining the beginning population (2020), final population (2022), net change in thousands of people, percent change, and average monthly change in thousands of people. The results are displayed in the table below:

```{r analyze-df-1d}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-1
#| tbl-cap: "US Top 10 States Population Growth (2020-2022)"

summary_1d <- df_1d |>
  group_by(area) |>
  summarize(
    start_pop_2020 = first(count),
    end_pop_2022 = last(count),
    net_change_k = (end_pop_2022-start_pop_2020)/1000,
    pct_change = (net_change_k)/(start_pop_2020/1000)*100,
    avg_monthly_k = mean(count_growth, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_change))

knitr::kable(summary_1d)
```

```{r setting-plot-theme}
#| echo:  false
#| warning:  false
#| message:  false

theme_standard <- function(){
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13, face = "italic"),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold")
    )
}
```

The US Census data is visualized in two plots, each showing the population change over the multi-year collection process. In the first, the total net population in thousands of people is shown.

```{r viz-summary-1d}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-1
#| fig-cap: "Net Population Change (April 2020 - July 2022)"

summary_1d |>
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(area, net_change_k), y = net_change_k, fill = net_change_k > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_standard() +
  labs(title = "Net Population Change (April 2020 - July 2022)",
       subtitle = "top 10 US states by population",
       x = "State",
       y = "Net Population Change (Thousands)") +
  coord_flip()

```

In the second, the percent population change of each of the top 10 US states is shown.

```{r viz-summary-1d-2}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-2
#| fig-cap: "Population Shift (April 2020 - July 2022)"

summary_1d |>
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(area, pct_change), y = pct_change, fill = net_change_k > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_standard() +
  labs(title = "Population Shift (April 2020 - July 2022)",
       subtitle = "top 10 US states by population",
       x = "State",
       y = "Percent Population Change (vs. April 2020)") +
  coord_flip()
```

### Data set 2: 2026 Business Performance

Business data is analyzed to determine total revenue, cost, and profit figures, as well as average profit per cost rates. The summary of this data is provided below:

```{r analyze-df-2c}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-2
#| tbl-cap: "2026 Business Performance Summary"

summary_2c <- df_2c |>
  group_by(name, location) |>
  summarize(
    total_revenue = sum(revenue),
    total_cost = sum(cost),
    total_profit = sum(profit),
    avg_ppc = mean(ppc, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(total_profit))

knitr::kable(summary_2c)

```

The monthly profit for each representative is visualized.

```{r viz-2c-1}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-3
#| fig-cap: "Monthly Profit Trajectory by Representative (2026)"

df_2c |>
  ggplot(aes(x=date, y=profit, color = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Profit Trajectory by Representative (2026)",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Net Profit ($)"
  ) +
  theme_standard()
```

### Data set 3: World Bank Life Expectancy

First, this data set is aggregated by region before summarizing, so rows without region or life expectancy observations are initially filtered out. The resulting data frame is then summarized by the mean of the life expectancy values for each region. The summary is displayed below:

```{r analyze-df-3d}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-3
#| tbl-cap: "Average Life Expectancy"

region_summary_3d <- df_3d |>
  filter(!is.na(region), !is.na(life_expectancy)) |>
  group_by(region, date) |>
  summarize(
    mean_le = mean(life_expectancy)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(date))

knitr::kable(head(region_summary_3d,7))
```

The first visualization shows the life expectancy trajectory for each World Bank region between 1960 and 2024.

```{r viz-df-3d-1}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-4
#| fig-cap: "Life Expectancy Trajectories by Global Region"

region_summary_3d |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, 
             y = mean_le, 
             color = region)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_standard() +
  labs(
    title = "Life Expectancy Trajectories by Global Region",
    subtitle = "1960-2024",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Life Expectancy (years)",
    color = "World Bank Region"
  )
```

A second visualization reveals the disparity in life expectancy by income group using a box-plot:

```{r viz-3d-2}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-5
#| fig-cap: "Global Life Expectancy Disparity by Income Group"

last_year = max(region_summary_3d$date)

country_df <- df_3d |>
  filter(!is.na(region), 
         !is.na(life_expectancy)) |>
  filter(date == last_year, 
         !is.na(income_group))

country_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(income_group, 
                         life_expectancy, 
                         FUN = median), 
             y = life_expectancy, 
             fill = income_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_standard() +
  labs(
    title = "Global Life Expectancy Disparity by Income Group",
    subtitle = year(last_year),
    x = "Income Group",
    y = "Life Expectancy at Birth (years)"
  ) +
  coord_flip()
```

## Findings and Recommendations

### Data set 1 (US Census)

The US Census data from 2020-2022 shows clear interstate migration patterns. States like Texas and Florida saw monthly influxes exceeding 25,000 people. With population changes of over 700,000 net people (@tbl-1 ), Florida and Texas also show the greatest net positive percentage changes of over 3.0%, respectively (@fig-2). Meanwhile, states like California, New York, and Illinois experienced net exoduses over the same period: California and New York each exceeded a net loss of over one half million people during this time frame (@fig-1), while New York exhibited the greatest percentage loss of over 2.5% from 2020 (@fig-2).

This project could be expanded in the future by incorporating more historical data (e.g. census data from before 2020). Aggregate population growth rates could be compared to stratified data by state.

### Data set 2 (2026 Business Performance)

The business data encountered in data set 2 required cleaning, tidying, and dealing with erroneous observations. After correcting for a data entry error, performance for each representative is visualized. While Bobby in Boston earned the highest total revenue and greatest profit (@tbl-2), Emma in Dallas was the most efficient representative, with a profit per cost ratio of 0.60. Heading into June 2026, the trajectory plot shows only one representative with a positive profit momentum, Denise (@fig-3). Conversely, the representative with the greatest negative momentum is Bobby, who had a high profit month in May.

Future work could investigate data validation at the site of data entry to obviate errors like Bobby from Boston's \$6M revenue month. Additionally, this project naturally expands as reporting from new months is added to the set. Lastly, the data could be aggregated by quarter and compared year-to-year to observe macro trends.

### Data set 3 (World Bank Life Expectancy)

Global life expectancy has increased dramatically in the over six decades since 1960. Each World Bank Region has demonstrated clear aggregate progress in elevating life expectancy (@fig-4). Notably, all World Bank regions experienced a regression in the immediate period following 2020. This may help illustrate the global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020. Summarizing this information reveals that the region with the highest 2024 life expectancy at birth is North America at 81.2 years, and the region with the lowest 2024 life expectancy at birth is Sub-Saharan Africa at 64.8 years ( @tbl-3). The disparity in life expectancy by income group shows a clear relationship between income level and life expectancy: as income increases, so does life expectancy (@fig-4).

Extending this work by dis-aggregating regions into subsidiary countries could reveal interesting intra-regional trends (e.g. northern countries in Sub-Saharan Africa display higher life expectancy growth rates than southern countries). Additionally, new indicators such as median income or per capita gross domestic product could be joined into the data set to make comparisons between income and life expectancy more numerical.
